title: Where to eat in San Francisco
gist: A personal San Francisco restaurant guide that, beyond the recommendations, uses the city's food scene to illustrate how high rent, restrictive housing and small-business regulation, and poor intra-city transit distort a local service economy — producing a barbell of ultra-cheap and ultra-expensive restaurants with a hollowed-out middle, and letting legacy incumbents (like Chinatown's Cantonese restaurants) survive on rent-controlled leases without competitive pressure.

themes.theme: How rent, regulation, and geography shape a local service economy

insights.claim: Smith attributes San Francisco's extremely high commercial rents to a combination of demand from the AI boom and the broader tech industry, restrictive housing development policy, desirable weather, and the city's geographically constrained, dense position at the core of the Bay Area metro.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Direct, dated author testimony that the AI investment boom is actively pushing up San Francisco commercial and residential costs as of mid-2026, relevant to SF/Bay Area real estate and cost-of-living inputs.
insights.quote: SF is one of the least affordable cities in the country, thanks to the AI boom, the tech industry in general, draconian restrictions on housing development, the unique and excellent weather, and the fact that it’s destined by geography to be the dense core of a major metro area.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'OK, but San Francisco is by far the densest'

insights.claim: Smith argues San Francisco is one of the hardest U.S. cities in which to start a small business, due to decades of regulatory red tape accumulated under the city's governance, which forces new restaurants to charge higher prices to cover the extra time and money required to open.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concrete, on-the-ground account of regulatory burden functioning as a cost pass-through to consumers and a barrier to entry, relevant to any thesis on California/SF business-formation friction or local-service-sector margins.
insights.quote: San Francisco is one of the hardest places to start a small business, thanks to decades of red tape accumulated under supposedly 'progressive' governance.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'OK, but San Francisco is by far the densest'

insights.claim: Smith says high rent combined with barriers to entry has pushed San Francisco's restaurant market into a double-peaked ('barbell') distribution — very cheap places (e.g., banh mi shops) alongside very expensive ones (e.g., $600-a-person restaurants) — with few mid-priced options for the middle-income diner.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A generalizable pattern for high-cost, high-regulation urban markets: expect a hollowed-out middle tier in consumer-facing local services, since only rent-shielded incumbents (cheap legacy leases) or premium operators (able to absorb costs) survive.
insights.quote: This means that SF food tends to be a sort of double-peaked distribution, with $600-a-person places like Benu and cheap banh mi places like L&G, but not a lot of mid-price places.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'That means if you’re going to start a restaurant'

insights.claim: Smith argues San Francisco's high rents have hollowed out the middle class, pricing out both the ethnic communities that support dense ethnic-food scenes (as in Los Angeles) and the bohemian/artist population that drives creative, affordable dining options.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A qualitative data point on SF demographic hollowing-out (middle-income and creative-class flight) consistent with broader Bay Area affordability/outmigration narratives.
insights.quote: The middle class has largely been priced out of the city, leaving it to the rich and the rent-controlled.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'SF’s stratospheric rent also probably exerts'

insights.claim: Unlike New York (good rail transit) or car-friendly cities like LA, San Francisco lacks both an effective intra-city train network and car-friendliness, so residents tend to stay within their own neighborhoods, which reduces competitive pressure between restaurants across the city and lets neighborhood incumbents serve mediocre 'standard fare' without needing to innovate.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A transferable micro-economic mechanism: poor local transit infrastructure segments consumer markets geographically, weakening competitive pressure and quality/innovation incentives for local businesses — applicable beyond restaurants to any city's local-services competitiveness analysis.
insights.quote: When people stay in their neighborhoods, restaurants aren’t competing with each other nearly as much; everyone just goes to their local spots. This reduces the incentive for restaurants to innovate, raise their quality, and differentiate themselves.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Everybody knows about SF’s rent problem'

insights.claim: Smith's prescriptions for improving San Francisco's restaurant scene are explicitly framed as general urban-policy fixes: build more housing, make Muni transit faster with better coverage, cut red tape to make small-business formation easier, and allow and encourage multi-level retail.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A concise YIMBY-style policy checklist the author considers the fix for San Francisco's cost and competitiveness problems — relevant context for tracking SF/California housing and zoning reform momentum.
insights.locator: bulleted list beginning 'So if you want to make San Francisco’s food scene better'

themes.theme: Market structure signals from the restaurant scene

insights.claim: Smith argues that perceptions of San Francisco having a worse restaurant scene than New York or LA are partly a statistical artifact of city size: NYC (8.58 million people) and LA (3.87 million) mechanically support far more restaurants than SF (826,000 people), so even at equal quality, larger cities will offer more good options that people notice and favor.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: A reusable selection-bias framework: comparing 'best options found' across markets of very different population size will systematically favor larger markets even absent any quality difference — applicable to any cross-market quality comparison (retail density, startup ecosystems, etc.).
insights.quote: So if the number of restaurants is generally proportional to the number of people, then even if quality were equivalent, we’d expect NYC to have more than ten times as many good restaurants as SF, and LA to have more than four times as many.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'There’s one obvious, overriding reason: city size'

insights.claim: Despite Chinese residents making up almost a quarter of San Francisco's population, Smith calls Chinese food the city's biggest culinary failing, dominated by mediocre Cantonese banquet restaurants that appear largely unchanged since the 1980s, particularly in Chinatown, which he attributes to incumbents surviving on old, cheap legacy leases without competitive pressure to improve.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: Another concrete instance of the rent-insulation-from-competition mechanism: legacy cheap-lease holders in Chinatown persist with low quality/investment despite a large addressable customer base, illustrating how rent control/legacy leases can entrench low-quality incumbents.
insights.quote: Instead, it has endless mediocre Cantonese banquet places that look like they haven’t changed a thing (including their signage and decor) since 1982... Chinatown is mostly dominated by incredibly mediocre antiquated places that are still hanging on to their ancient cheap leases.
insights.locator: paragraph beginning 'Chinese food is undoubtedly San Francisco’s biggest culinary failing'

insights.claim: Smith describes San Francisco's SoMa neighborhood as a 'great food desert' whose restaurant scene has still not recovered from the pandemic: it once thrived on daytime office workers, but COVID emptied downtown, closing most lunch and happy-hour spots, and even with workers slowly returning, the neighborhood's food scene remains diminished.
insights.speaker: Noah Smith
insights.so_what: First-hand, dated (as of August 2026) evidence that San Francisco's downtown office-district service economy still has not fully recovered from pandemic-era remote work shifts, relevant to office-to-downtown-retail recovery timelines in major US urban cores.
insights.quote: SoMa: San Francisco’s great food desert. It was once the center of SF’s bustling daytime office culture... Then Covid hit, and everyone left downtown, and the takeaway spots and happy hour bars closed down. Now workers are slowly coming back to the area, but it’ll take a while for the neighborhood restaurant scene to recover.
insights.locator: paragraph on SoMa in Neighborhoods section
